content: The non-negative integers are often represented in two ways: one conventionally used in number theory and the other preferred in mathematical logic, set theory, and computer science. A more formal definition will be provided later. Natural numbers serve two primary purposes: they are used for counting (e.g., there are 3 apples on the table) and for ordering (e.g., this is the 3rd largest city in the country). Properties of natural numbers related to divisibility, such as the distribution of prime numbers, are studied in number theory. Problems involving counting, such as those in Ramsey theory, are explored in combinatorics. History of Natural Numbers and the Status of Zero The concept of natural numbers originated from the words used to count objects, starting with the number one. The first significant abstraction was the use of numerals to represent numbers, enabling systems for recording large quantities. For instance, the Babylonians developed a powerful place-value system based on the numerals for 1 and 10. The ancient Egyptians used a numeral system with distinct hieroglyphs for 1, 10, and all powers of 10 up to one million. A stone carving from Karnak, dating to around 1500 BC and now housed in the Louvre, depicts the number 276 as 2 hundreds, 7 tens, and 6 ones, and similarly for the number 4,622. A much later advancement in abstraction was the development of the concept of zero as a number with its own numeral. A zero digit was used in place-value notation as early as 700 BC by the Babylonians, though they omitted it when it would have been the last symbol in a number. The Olmec and Maya civilizations independently developed the use of zero as a separate number as early as the 1st century BC, but this usage did not spread beyond Mesoamerica. The modern concept of zero originated with the Indian mathematician Brahmagupta in 628 AD. However, medieval computists (calculators of Easter), starting with Dionysius Exiguus in 525 AD, used zero as a number without employing a Roman numeral to represent it. Instead, they used the Latin word nullus, meaning nothing. The systematic study of numbers as abstract entities is generally attributed to the Greek philosophers Pythagoras and Archimedes. However, independent studies also occurred around the same time in India, China, and Mesoamerica. In the 19th century, a set-theoretical definition of natural numbers was developed. This definition conveniently included zero (corresponding to the empty set) as a natural number. Including zero in the natural numbers is now the standard convention among set theorists, logicians, and computer scientists. However, some mathematicians, such as number theorists, adhere to the older tradition and consider 1 to be the first natural number. Notation Mathematicians use the symbol ( mathbb{N} ) (a blackboard bold N) to denote the set of all natural numbers. This set is countably infinite, meaning it is infinite but can be counted by definition. The cardinality of this set is expressed as ( aleph_0 ) (aleph-null). To clarify whether zero is included, some notations add an index 0 for inclusion (e.g., ( mathbb{N}_0 )) or a superscript for exclusion (e.g., ( mathbb{N}^ )). In some cases, a + is used to signify positive integers. Set theorists often denote the set of all natural numbers by the lowercase Greek letter omega (( omega )), which explicitly includes zero as a natural number. Algebraic Properties The natural numbers can be formally defined using the Peano axioms, which establish the foundational properties of these numbers. These axioms include the existence of a natural number 0, the existence of a successor for every natural number, and the principle of mathematical induction. The Peano axioms ensure that the natural numbers are well-defined and consistent. Addition and multiplication can be recursively defined on the natural numbers. For example, addition is defined such that ( a + 0 = a ) and ( a + S(b) = S(a + b) ), where ( S(b) ) denotes the successor of ( b ). Similarly, multiplication is defined such that ( a times 0 = 0 ) and ( a times S(b) = (a times b) + a ). These operations make the natural numbers a commutative semiring, with addition and multiplication satisfying the distributive property. The natural numbers are well-ordered, meaning every non-empty subset of natural numbers has a least element. This property is fundamental in mathematics and is expressed by the ordinal number ( omega ). While division is not always possible within the natural numbers, the division algorithm allows for division with a remainder. For any two natural numbers ( a ) and ( b ) (with ( b neq 0 )), there exist unique natural numbers ( q ) (quotient) and ( r ) (remainder) such that ( a = bq + r ) and ( 0 leq r < b ). Generalizations Natural numbers can be generalized in two ways: 1. Cardinal Numbers: These measure the size of a set, including infinite sets. The cardinality of the set of natural numbers and any countably infinite set is ( aleph_0 ). 2. Ordinal Numbers: These describe the position of an element in a well-ordered set. The first ordinal number that is not a natural number is ( omega ), which is also the ordinal number of the set of natural numbers itself. For finite well-ordered sets, there is a one-to-one correspondence between ordinal and cardinal numbers, allowing both to be expressed by the same natural number. This number represents both the size of the set and the position of an element within it.
